questions.question: What is the mandatory entry point function where execution begins in every standard C program?
questions.explanation: In ISO C, program execution begins at main(). It typically returns int to indicate exit status.

questions.question: Which preprocessor directive is required to import the standard input/output header in C?
questions.explanation: #include <stdio.h> directs the preprocessor to paste the standard I/O library declarations.

questions.question: Which escape sequence creates a newline in printf() output?
questions.explanation: \n places a newline character into the output stream, moving the cursor to the start of the next line.

questions.question: Which syntax denotes a multi-line comment in C?
questions.explanation: Multi-line comments start with /* and end with */. Single line comments start with //.

questions.question: What happens if you omit the semicolon at the end of a statement in C?
questions.a: The compiler assumes a default value
questions.b: The compiler issues a syntax error
questions.c: The runtime engine inserts a semicolon
questions.explanation: C uses semicolons as mandatory statement terminators; omitting one produces a compile-time syntax error.

questions.question: What is the return value of main() typically interpreted as by the operating system?
questions.a: Heap memory allocation size in bytes
questions.b: Execution status code to the environment
questions.explanation: Returning 0 signifies successful execution, while non-zero values report error states to the OS.

questions.question: Which format specifier is used to display a single character in printf()?
questions.explanation: %c is for single char values. %s is for null-terminated strings.

questions.question: What is the typical memory footprint of a standard float in modern C?
questions.explanation: Single-precision IEEE 754 floats take 4 bytes (32 bits), while doubles take 8 bytes (64 bits).

questions.question: Which format specifier is used to print a double with printf()?
questions.explanation: In printf(), %f handles both float and double (due to default argument promotion).

questions.question: What is the result of evaluating: int x = (int) 7.95; ?
questions.explanation: Explicit cast to int truncates the decimal fraction towards zero, yielding 7 without rounding.

questions.question: What format specifier must be passed to scanf() when reading into a double variable?
questions.explanation: Unlike printf(), scanf() expects %lf for a double pointer and %f for a float pointer.

questions.question: What is the value of char ch = 65; when printed with printf("%c", ch)?
questions.explanation: ASCII code 65 represents the uppercase character 'A'.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to declare a variable whose value cannot be reassigned?
questions.explanation: The const qualifier marks an identifier as read-only after initialization.

questions.question: What is the operator for calculating the integer division remainder in C?
questions.explanation: The modulo operator % yields the integer remainder (e.g., 7 % 3 evaluates to 1).

questions.question: What is the difference between prefix ++x and postfix x++ in an expression?
questions.a: Prefix increments before evaluation; postfix increments after
questions.b: Postfix increments before evaluation; prefix increments after
questions.c: Prefix operates on floats; postfix operates on integers only
questions.d: There is no functional difference in any evaluation context
questions.explanation: ++x increments x and yields the new value; x++ evaluates to the current value then increments.

questions.question: Which bitwise operator performs a bitwise XOR operation between two operands?
questions.explanation: ^ is bitwise XOR, & is bitwise AND, | is bitwise OR, and ~ is bitwise NOT.

questions.question: What does the sizeof operator evaluate to when applied to an expression?
questions.a: The memory size in bits as an unsigned integer
questions.b: The memory size in bytes as type size_t
questions.c: The number of items stored in dynamic heap memory
questions.d: The current stack address offset of the variable
questions.explanation: sizeof yields the object size in bytes as an unsigned integral type named size_t.

questions.question: What is the value of expression: 5 + 2 * 4 in standard C?
questions.explanation: Multiplication has higher precedence than addition: 2 * 4 = 8, then 5 + 8 = 13.

questions.question: Which header must be included to use the bool, true, and false keywords in standard C99?
questions.explanation: <stdbool.h> defines bool as a macro for _Bool, along with true (1) and false (0).

questions.question: In C condition evaluation, which integer value is treated as false?
questions.explanation: In C, exactly 0 evaluates to false; any non-zero value evaluates to true.

questions.question: What does the ternary operator (? :) return in: int z = (10 > 5) ? 100 : 200; ?
questions.explanation: Since 10 > 5 is true, the expression evaluates to the expression before the colon (100).

questions.question: What is the result of expression: (0 && printf("Hello")) in C?
questions.b: Prints nothing due to logical short-circuit
questions.explanation: Logical AND (&&) short-circuits: because the left operand is 0, the right side is never evaluated.

questions.question: What is the output of: if (x = 0) printf("A"); else printf("B"); ?
questions.explanation: x = 0 assigns 0 to x and evaluates to 0 (false), directing control to the else branch.

questions.question: Which logical operator represents logical OR in C?
questions.explanation: || is logical OR. Single | is bitwise OR.

questions.question: What happens if a matching case in a switch statement does not contain a break statement?
questions.a: Execution terminates immediately with status code zero
questions.b: Execution falls through to subsequent case statements
questions.c: The compiler generates a mandatory fatal error
questions.d: The switch restarts evaluation from the default case
questions.explanation: Without break, control continues sequentially into subsequent cases (fallthrough).

questions.question: Which data type is NOT allowed as the control expression in a C switch statement?
questions.explanation: Switch expressions in C must evaluate to integral types (int, char, enum). Floating points are disallowed.

questions.question: Which clause in a switch statement executes when no case constant matches the expression?
questions.explanation: default specifies the fallback block executed when no case value matches.

questions.question: Can case values in a switch statement be variables (e.g. case x:)?
questions.a: Yes, if declared before the switch statement block
questions.b: No, case labels must be integer constant expressions
questions.c: Yes, only if x is passed as a function argument
questions.d: Yes, but only inside GNU GCC compiler extensions
questions.explanation: C case labels must be compile-time constant integral expressions.

questions.question: Is the default clause required to be positioned as the last item in a switch statement?
questions.a: Yes, placing it anywhere else causes syntax error
questions.b: No, it can appear anywhere in the switch body
questions.c: Yes, because it terminates the switch execution flow
questions.d: No, but it will only execute if written first
questions.explanation: default can appear at any position inside the switch statement, though placing it last is conventional.

questions.question: Can two different case labels share the same integer constant in one switch?
questions.a: Yes, if they execute identical code statements
questions.b: No, duplicate case values cause a compilation error
questions.c: Yes, the runtime picks the first matching label
questions.d: Yes, if separated by a default clause boundary
questions.explanation: Duplicate case constants in the same switch block produce a duplicate case value compiler error.

questions.question: How many times does the body of a do-while loop execute at minimum?
questions.explanation: do-while checks its condition at the bottom, guaranteeing at least one execution.

questions.question: What is the effect of the continue statement inside a loop body?
questions.b: Skips remainder of current iteration and tests condition
questions.c: Restarts the loop from index zero
questions.d: Pauses execution for one clock cycle
questions.explanation: continue bypasses remaining statements in the current iteration and jumps to the loop update/condition.

questions.question: What happens when executing: for (;;) { ... } in C?
questions.a: Generates a syntax error due to missing expressions
questions.b: Creates an infinite loop unless exited via break/return
questions.c: Executes exactly zero times and exits immediately
questions.d: Causes a stack overflow compilation crash
questions.explanation: Omitting all three expressions in for (;;) is standard C syntax for an infinite loop.

questions.question: How many times will this loop print: for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) printf("X"); ?
questions.explanation: i takes values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (5 total iterations). When i reaches 5, condition i < 5 becomes false.

questions.question: What does the break statement do when executed inside an inner nested loop?
questions.a: Terminates all outer enclosing loops at once
questions.b: Exits only the innermost loop containing the break
questions.c: Pauses both loops until user input arrives
questions.d: Jumps to the main() function return statement
questions.explanation: break exits only the immediately enclosing switch or loop construct.

questions.question: What is the final value of x after: int x = 0; while (x < 10) x += 3; ?
questions.explanation: x sequences 0 -> 3 -> 6 -> 9 -> 12. At 12, x < 10 is false, so the loop terminates with x = 12.

questions.question: What is the index of the first element in any C array?
questions.explanation: C uses 0-based array indexing. The first element of array arr is arr[0].

questions.question: If int arr[5] = {1, 2}; is declared, what is the value of arr[3]?
questions.explanation: When an array initializer list provides fewer values than array length, remaining elements are set to 0.

questions.question: How do you calculate the number of elements in array int arr[20] using sizeof?
questions.explanation: Total array bytes divided by single element bytes yields total element count.

questions.question: How are elements of a 2D array matrix[3][4] arranged in physical RAM?
questions.c: In fragmented heap chunks via pointers
questions.d: In reverse stack order by row
questions.explanation: C arrays are laid out in contiguous memory using row-major ordering.

questions.question: What occurs if your code writes past the declared bounds of an array in C?
questions.a: The compiler automatically extends the array memory
questions.b: Undefined behavior potentially causing memory corruption
questions.c: The OS throws an ArrayOutOfBoundsException error
questions.d: The program pauses and prompts user for memory
questions.explanation: C has no built-in array bounds checking; out-of-bounds writes invoke undefined behavior (UB).

questions.question: For int matrix[2][3] = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}};, what is matrix[1][0]?
questions.explanation: Row index 1 refers to the second row {4, 5, 6}, and column 0 is 4.

questions.question: What special character marks the end of a valid string in C?
questions.explanation: C strings are null-terminated character sequences ending in '\0' (ASCII 0).

questions.question: Which function from <string.h> returns the character count of a string excluding '\0'?
questions.explanation: strlen() counts characters up to (but not including) the null terminator.

questions.question: What is the return value of strcmp("apple", "apple")?
questions.explanation: strcmp() returns 0 when both strings are lexicographically identical.

questions.question: Which function safely appends one string to the end of another in C?
questions.explanation: strcat(dest, src) concatenates src onto dest (dest must have adequate allocated buffer).

questions.question: What is the minimum array size needed to store the string "Hello" including null terminator?
questions.explanation: "Hello" has 5 printable letters + 1 null terminator '\0' = 6 bytes minimum.

questions.question: Why is strcpy() considered unsafe compared to strncpy()?
questions.a: It converts all characters to lowercase silently
questions.b: It does not check destination buffer capacity limits
questions.c: It cannot copy strings containing numeric digits
questions.d: It requires dynamic heap memory allocation to copy
questions.explanation: strcpy() copies until '\0' without checking bounds, risking buffer overflow exploits.

questions.question: Why must the & address-of operator be passed before non-pointer variables in scanf()?
questions.a: To allow scanf() to write data directly into the variable address
questions.b: To convert the variable to a read-only constant during input
questions.c: To allocate new dynamic heap memory for the incoming input
questions.d: To instruct the compiler to verify the variable data type
questions.explanation: C uses pass-by-value; scanf() needs memory addresses to write parsed input back to caller variables.

questions.question: Why does scanf("%s", str) fail when reading full sentences like "Hello World"?
questions.a: It aborts on non-alphabetical punctuation symbols
questions.b: It stops reading at the first whitespace character
questions.c: It only accepts string inputs up to four bytes
questions.d: It converts all spaces into null terminators
questions.explanation: %s in scanf treats spaces, tabs, and newlines as input delimiters.

questions.question: Which function safely reads an entire line including spaces from standard input?
questions.explanation: fgets(buffer, size, stdin) reads up to size-1 characters safely avoiding buffer overflow.

questions.question: What is the return value of scanf() upon successful execution?
questions.a: Total number of bytes consumed from input stream
questions.b: Number of input items successfully assigned
questions.c: Zero on all successful input read operations
questions.d: Memory address pointer of the destination buffer
questions.explanation: scanf() returns the count of input items successfully matched and assigned.

questions.question: Which standard function writes a single character to standard output?
questions.explanation: putchar(ch) writes a single character to standard output (stdout).

questions.question: Why is the legacy gets() function removed from modern C standards (C11)?
questions.a: It does not support modern UTF-8 string encoding
questions.b: It has no buffer limit check and causes severe security flaws
questions.c: It requires operating system administrative privileges
questions.d: It was superseded by the printf() formatting engine
questions.explanation: gets() cannot prevent buffer overflows because it has no length parameter, so C11 removed it.

questions.question: What does a function return type of void signify?
questions.a: The function returns a generic void* pointer
questions.b: The function does not return any value to caller
questions.c: The function terminates the entire program
questions.d: The function takes no parameter arguments
questions.explanation: void as return type indicates that no value is returned to the caller.

questions.question: What is the default argument passing mechanism in C functions?
questions.explanation: C exclusively uses pass-by-value; copies of arguments are passed to function parameters.

questions.question: What is a function prototype (forward declaration)?
questions.a: The complete machine code compiled binary
questions.b: A declaration informing the compiler of function signature before definition
questions.c: A macro that replaces function calls inline
questions.d: A special function that executes before main()
questions.explanation: Prototypes declare name, parameters, and return type so the compiler can validate calls before full definition.

questions.question: What happens to a local variable declared inside a function when the function returns?
questions.a: It is persisted permanently in global static memory
questions.b: Its stack frame memory is reclaimed and destroyed
questions.c: It is automatically migrated into heap storage
questions.d: It remains accessible through its original name
questions.explanation: Automatic local variables have automatic storage duration on the stack and expire upon function exit.

questions.question: What is the effect of declaring a local variable with the static keyword inside a function?
questions.a: It retains its value across multiple function calls
questions.b: It makes the variable immutable like a constant
questions.c: It allocates the variable on the runtime heap
questions.d: It allows other source files to access the variable
questions.explanation: static local variables are initialized once and preserve state between successive function invocations.

questions.question: What must every recursive function contain to avoid infinite recursion and stack overflow?
questions.a: At least one dynamic malloc allocation call
questions.b: A base case condition that terminates recursion
questions.c: A loop statement iterating over arguments
questions.d: A static local counter variable definition
questions.explanation: A base case returns without making further recursive calls, preventing stack overflow.

questions.question: What does the & operator return when placed before a variable name?
questions.a: The value stored in the variable
questions.b: The memory address of the variable
questions.c: The size of the variable in bytes
questions.d: A pointer to the next array element
questions.explanation: The & (address-of) operator yields the physical memory location of an lvalue.

questions.question: What operation is performed by *ptr when ptr is a pointer holding a valid memory address?
questions.b: Dereferencing to access value at address
questions.d: Incrementing the address stored in ptr
questions.explanation: The unary * operator dereferences a pointer, reading or modifying the value stored at the pointed address.

questions.question: If ptr points to an int on a system with 4-byte integers, what does ptr + 1 point to?
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic scales by sizeof(type). ptr + 1 advances the address by sizeof(int) = 4 bytes.

questions.question: What does malloc() return if the operating system has insufficient memory to satisfy the request?
questions.d: A pointer to swap disk space
questions.explanation: malloc returns NULL upon allocation failure. Code should always verify ptr != NULL before use.

questions.question: What is the critical difference between malloc() and calloc()?
questions.a: malloc() allocates on stack; calloc() allocates on heap
questions.b: calloc() initializes allocated memory to zero; malloc() does not
questions.c: malloc() is faster because it automatically frees memory
questions.d: calloc() can only allocate character array memory blocks
questions.explanation: calloc(n, size) clears all allocated bytes to zero; malloc(size) leaves memory uninitialized.

questions.question: What is a dangling pointer?
questions.a: A pointer initialized to NULL address
questions.b: A pointer referencing memory that has been freed
questions.c: A pointer pointing to a global variable
questions.d: A void pointer with no associated data type
questions.explanation: A dangling pointer holds the address of deallocated or out-of-scope memory.

questions.question: How do you access a structure member through a pointer struct Student *s?
questions.explanation: The arrow operator s->name is syntactic shorthand for (*s).name.

questions.question: What is the primary memory difference between struct and union in C?
questions.a: Struct members share memory; union members are separate
questions.b: Union members share same memory; struct members are separate
questions.c: Structs are allocated on heap; unions are on stack
questions.d: Unions cannot store pointer data type members
questions.explanation: In union, all members overlay the same memory space (size = largest member). Struct members have separate offsets.

questions.question: Which fopen() mode opens a file for writing, discarding existing content or creating a new file?
questions.explanation: "w" opens for writing and truncates existing file content to zero length or creates a new file.

questions.question: What does fopen() return when the specified file path cannot be opened?
questions.explanation: fopen() returns a NULL pointer if it fails to open or create the file.

questions.question: What does typedef do in C?
questions.a: Allocates a new structure on heap storage
questions.b: Creates an alias name for an existing data type
questions.c: Restricts variable mutation like const qualifier
questions.d: Imports external types from external headers
questions.explanation: typedef creates synonym aliases for existing types (e.g. typedef unsigned long ulong;).

questions.question: What is the default integer value assigned to the first identifier in an enum if unassigned?
questions.explanation: Enum constants start at 0 by default and increment by 1 for each subsequent member.

questions.question: Which function must always be called to flush buffers and release file handles opened with fopen()?
questions.explanation: fclose(fp) flushes internal stream buffers and closes OS file descriptor handles.

questions.question: Which header file must be included to use functions like sqrt(), pow(), and ceil()?
questions.explanation: The <math.h> header contains declarations for standard mathematical functions in C.

questions.question: What is the return value of the function call ceil(4.2)?
questions.explanation: The ceil() function rounds a floating-point number UP to the nearest integer.

questions.question: How does the floor() function behave when given a negative number like -3.4?
questions.explanation: floor() rounds DOWN to the nearest integer. For negative numbers, rounding down moves further away from zero.

questions.question: Which operator is used to access a member of a struct variable directly (not through a pointer)?
questions.explanation: The dot (.) operator accesses members of a standard struct variable, while the arrow (->) is used for struct pointers.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax to declare an array of 10 'Student' structs?
questions.explanation: In C, you combine the struct keyword, the tag name (Student), the variable name (arr), and the array size [10].

questions.question: If 'arr' is an integer array, what is the pointer arithmetic equivalent of accessing arr[2]?
questions.explanation: In C, the array name acts as a pointer to its first element. *(arr + 2) dereferences the address two integer spaces ahead of the base.

questions.question: Which function allows you to safely resize a previously allocated block of dynamic memory?
questions.explanation: realloc() changes the size of a previously allocated memory block, moving it to a new location if necessary to find contiguous space.

questions.question: What happens if realloc() fails to find enough contiguous memory to expand a block?
questions.b: It returns NULL and leaves the original memory block untouched
questions.c: It automatically deletes the old block and returns NULL
questions.d: It returns a pointer to the hard drive's swap space
questions.explanation: If realloc fails, it returns NULL. Developers must check for NULL before overwriting the original pointer to avoid memory leaks.

questions.question: Which function is used to write formatted text data to a file stream?
questions.explanation: fprintf() operates exactly like printf(), but requires a file pointer as its first argument to direct the output to a file.

questions.question: When reading from a file using fgetc(), what special macro represents the end of the file?
questions.explanation: EOF (End Of File) is a macro defined in <stdio.h> (usually as -1) returned when there is no more data to read.

questions.question: Which function allows you to read an entire line of text from a file safely into a buffer?
questions.explanation: fgets() reads up to a specified number of characters from a file stream, stopping at a newline or EOF, preventing buffer overflows.

questions.question: What programming paradigm does standard C strictly follow?
questions.explanation: C is a procedural language; it executes sequences of statements, manipulating state directly via functions and variables.

questions.question: What is the correct sequence of the standard C compilation pipeline?
questions.explanation: The pipeline runs: Preprocessor (handles # directives), Compiler (translates to assembly), Assembler (translates to machine code), Linker (combines object files).

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between a compilation error and a runtime error?
questions.a: Compilation errors happen on Windows; runtime errors happen on Linux
questions.b: Compilation errors prevent the executable from being created; runtime errors crash the executable while it is running
questions.c: Compilation errors are caused by hardware; runtime errors are caused by software
questions.explanation: Syntax issues cause compilation errors. Logic flaws (like dividing by zero or bad pointers) cause runtime errors after the program starts.

questions.question: Where are local, non-static variables stored during a function's execution?
questions.explanation: Local variables with automatic storage duration are pushed onto the Call Stack and are destroyed when the function returns.

questions.question: What does 'endianness' refer to in computer architecture?
questions.a: The maximum memory limit of a C program
questions.b: The byte order used to store multi-byte data types in memory
questions.c: The speed of the CPU cache
questions.d: The process of closing file streams
questions.explanation: Endianness (Big-Endian vs Little-Endian) determines whether the most significant or least significant byte is stored at the lowest memory address.

questions.question: What is an algorithm in the context of programming?
questions.b: A step-by-step set of operations to solve a specific problem
questions.d: A tool used strictly for finding bugs
questions.explanation: An algorithm is a finite sequence of rigorous instructions, independent of any specific programming language.

questions.question: In standard ASCII representation, how is character data actually stored in computer memory?
questions.b: As numeric integer values ranging from 0 to 127
questions.explanation: Computers only understand numbers. ASCII maps characters to integers (e.g., 'A' is stored as the integer 65).

questions.question: Why do C programmers frequently use hexadecimal (Base-16) notation for memory addresses and bitwise masks?
questions.a: It executes faster on modern processors
questions.b: It is the only format the compiler understands
questions.c: It maps perfectly to binary, where one hex digit represents exactly four binary bits
questions.d: It consumes less memory space on the heap
questions.explanation: Hexadecimal is a highly readable shorthand for binary. One hex digit (0-F) perfectly represents a 4-bit nibble (0000-1111).

questions.question: What is the smallest addressable unit of memory in a standard modern computer architecture?
questions.explanation: While a bit is the smallest data unit, a byte (8 bits) is the smallest unit of memory that has its own address in C.

questions.question: What defines a 'side effect' in a programming expression?
questions.a: When an expression calculates a value but fails to return it
questions.b: When a function modifies some state outside its local environment, like a global variable or I/O stream
questions.c: When a program crashes due to a segmentation fault
questions.d: When a compiler optimization ignores unused variables
questions.explanation: A side effect occurs when an expression changes the observable state of the program, such as modifying a file, printing to the screen, or changing a global variable.

questions.question: What is the exact result of executing: int a = 5; int b = a++ + ++a; in ISO C?
questions.a: Always exactly 12 across all standard compilers
questions.b: Always exactly 13 across all standard compilers
questions.c: Undefined behavior due to multiple unsequenced modifications
questions.d: Compile-time syntax error on arithmetic addition
questions.explanation: Modifying a scalar object more than once between sequence points without intervening sequencing invokes Undefined Behavior (UB).

questions.question: Consider char *p = "hello"; p[0] = 'H';. What happens at runtime on modern operating systems?
questions.a: p[0] becomes 'H' successfully in read-write memory
questions.b: Segmentation fault / bus error writing to read-only string literal
questions.c: String is copied to stack automatically before modification
questions.d: Compiler truncates the string to single character 'H'
questions.explanation: String literals are stored in read-only text/data sections. Attempting to mutate them via char* causes a segmentation fault.

questions.question: What does the declaration void (*signal(int sig, void (*func)(int)))(int); define?
questions.a: A pointer to an array of function pointers returning integers
questions.b: A function taking int and func pointer, returning a func pointer
questions.c: A recursive macro expanding to POSIX signal handler prototypes
questions.d: A syntax error under ANSI C89 and modern C99 compilers
questions.explanation: signal is a function accepting an int and a function pointer (taking int, returning void), which returns a pointer to a function taking int and returning void.

questions.question: What is the strict aliasing rule in C (ISO C99 Section 6.5)?
questions.a: Pointers of different types cannot point to the same memory unless one is char*
questions.b: Two pointer variables cannot share the same variable identifier name
questions.c: Struct members must align strictly to 64-bit boundaries in heap memory
questions.d: Functions cannot accept both float and double pointer parameters together
questions.explanation: Strict aliasing states that two pointers of incompatible types cannot alias the same memory (with exceptions like char* and compatible signed/unsigned types), enabling aggressive compiler optimizations.

questions.question: What does free(ptr) do to the address stored inside the pointer variable ptr itself?
questions.a: Automatically assigns NULL to ptr in caller scope
questions.b: Leaves ptr holding the deallocated memory address (dangling pointer)
questions.c: Zeroes the 8 bytes of stack storage where ptr lives
questions.d: Deallocates ptr variable stack storage immediately
questions.explanation: free() receives the pointer address by value and releases the heap chunk. It cannot modify the caller pointer variable, leaving it dangling.

questions.question: What does the 'return 0;' statement at the end of the main() function typically signal to the operating system?
questions.a: The program encountered an unrecoverable error
questions.b: The program executed and terminated successfully with exit code 0
questions.c: The program should loop back to the beginning
questions.d: Zero bytes of memory were allocated
questions.explanation: Returning 0 from main() indicates successful program execution (EXIT_SUCCESS) to the parent shell process.

questions.question: In C, which punctuation character is strictly required to terminate every simple statement?
questions.explanation: Statements in C must end with a semicolon (;) to mark the completion of the statement instruction.

questions.question: Which of the following represents a valid multi-line comment in standard C?
questions.explanation: C supports block comments enclosed within /* and */, as well as C99 single-line comments prefixed by //.

questions.question: What is the primary role of the C Preprocessor (cpp)?
questions.a: To execute the compiled binary executable
questions.b: To handle macro expansions (#define), file inclusions (#include), and conditional compilation (#ifdef) before compilation begins
questions.explanation: The preprocessor processes all directives beginning with '#' before lexical analysis and compilation occur.

questions.question: Which compiler toolchain command compiles a source file 'main.c' into an executable named 'app' using GCC?
questions.explanation: The -o flag in GCC / Clang specifies the target output binary filename.

questions.question: What file extension is standard for C header interface files?
questions.explanation: Header files containing function prototypes, macros, and struct definitions use the .h extension.

questions.question: What does the escape sequence '\n' represent in a C string literal?
questions.explanation: The '\n' escape character moves the console output cursor to the beginning of the next line.

questions.question: What does the escape sequence '\t' represent in C?
questions.explanation: '\t' advances output to the next horizontal tab stop (typically 4 or 8 spaces).

questions.question: Which standard library function is used to print formatted text to the standard output console?
questions.explanation: printf() from <stdio.h> prints formatted character streams to stdout.

questions.question: What is the role of the Linker in the C build process?
questions.b: Combines compiled object files (.o/.obj) and external library routines into a final runnable executable binary
questions.explanation: The linker resolves external symbol references across object files and standard runtime libraries (libc).

questions.question: What is the typical size of a standard 'char' data type in ISO C?
questions.explanation: In C, sizeof(char) is strictly guaranteed to be exactly 1 byte.

questions.question: Which format specifier is used in printf() to print a floating-point number with double precision ('double')?
questions.explanation: %f is used for double/float in printf(), while %lf is explicitly required for double in scanf().

questions.question: Which format specifier is used to print an unsigned integer in hexadecimal format (lowercase)?
questions.explanation: %x formats unsigned integer values as lowercase hexadecimal (e.g. 0x2a); %X produces uppercase.

questions.question: What is the minimum value an 'unsigned int' can hold?
questions.explanation: Unsigned integer types can only represent non-negative numbers, with a minimum value of 0.

questions.question: Which keyword in C is used to define an alias or alternative name for an existing data type?
questions.explanation: typedef creates synonymous identifiers for data types (e.g. typedef unsigned long ulong;).

questions.question: What does the 'sizeof' operator return in C?
questions.a: The number of elements in a dynamically allocated array
questions.b: The memory size of a type or variable in bytes (as size_t)
questions.c: The number of bits in a register
questions.d: The memory address of the variable
questions.explanation: sizeof evaluates the storage size in bytes required for an object representation.

questions.question: Which standard header must be included to use fixed-width integer types like 'uint32_t' and 'int64_t' in C99?
questions.explanation: <stdint.h> provides exact-width integer types guaranteed across all hardware architectures.

questions.question: What happens when an integer variable exceeds its maximum representable positive value (Integer Overflow) in signed arithmetic?
questions.a: It raises a compile-time fatal exception
questions.b: Signed integer overflow invokes Undefined Behavior in ISO C
questions.c: It automatically converts to a floating point number
questions.explanation: Signed overflow is undefined behavior in ISO C, whereas unsigned overflow wraps modulo 2^N.

questions.question: What type does the literal '3.14' default to in C if no suffix is appended?
questions.explanation: Floating-point literals without suffixes (like 3.14) are typed as double. Use 3.14f for single-precision float.

questions.question: Which type qualifier prevents a variable from being modified after its initial assignment?
questions.explanation: const marks a variable as read-only, causing compiler errors if reassigned.

questions.question: What is the difference between prefix increment (++x) and postfix increment (x++) in an expression?
questions.a: Prefix increments the value before evaluating the expression; postfix evaluates the current value first, then increments
questions.c: Prefix works only on pointers; postfix works on integers
questions.d: There is no functional difference in C
questions.explanation: ++x returns the incremented result immediately, while x++ yields the original value before mutating x.

questions.question: What is the result of integer division '7 / 2' in C?
questions.explanation: Integer division truncates any fractional remainder, returning 3.

questions.question: Which operator returns the remainder of an integer division in C?
questions.explanation: The % modulo operator computes the remainder (e.g. 7 % 2 == 1).

questions.question: What is the bitwise AND operator in C?
questions.explanation: & is bitwise AND (operating on individual binary bits), while && is logical boolean AND.

questions.question: What is the bitwise XOR (Exclusive OR) operator in C?
questions.explanation: ^ performs bitwise XOR, returning 1 when operand bits differ and 0 when they match.

questions.question: What does the left bit-shift operator 'x << 1' effectively do to an integer x (assuming no overflow)?
questions.explanation: Shifting binary bits left by 1 position doubles the integer value (multiplication by 2^n).

questions.question: What is the ternary conditional operator syntax in C?
questions.a: if condition then x else y
questions.explanation: The ternary operator (? :) evaluates to expression_true if condition is non-zero, else expression_false.

questions.question: What does the comma operator ',' do in a compound C expression?
questions.b: Evaluates the left operand, discards the result, then evaluates and returns the right operand
questions.c: Combines two values into an array
questions.explanation: The comma operator evaluates expressions sequentially from left to right, yielding the value of the rightmost operand.

questions.question: Which operator has higher precedence in C: Multiplication (*) or Addition (+)?
questions.explanation: Multiplication, division, and modulo have higher precedence than binary addition and subtraction.

questions.question: What is the value of '!0' (logical NOT zero) in C?
questions.explanation: In C, zero represents false; logical NOT on zero evaluates to 1 (true).

questions.question: In C, how are truth values evaluated in conditional if() statements?
questions.b: Zero (0) is FALSE; ANY non-zero value (positive or negative) is TRUE
questions.c: Only boolean true objects are valid
questions.explanation: Any non-zero numerical evaluation is treated as true in control flow expressions.

questions.question: Which header must be included in C99 to use the 'bool', 'true', and 'false' identifiers?
questions.explanation: <stdbool.h> defines bool as _Bool, true as 1, and false as 0.

questions.question: What is 'Short-Circuit Evaluation' in logical expressions (&& and ||)?
questions.a: The second operand is only evaluated if the first operand does not determine the outcome
questions.b: Both operands are evaluated concurrently in hardware
questions.explanation: In 'A && B', if A is false, B is never evaluated. In 'A || B', if A is true, B is skipped.

questions.question: What is a common semantic bug when writing 'if (x = 5)' instead of 'if (x == 5)'?
questions.b: It assigns 5 to x and always evaluates as TRUE (because 5 is non-zero)
questions.explanation: = is assignment; == is equality comparison. 'x = 5' assigns 5, which evaluates to non-zero (true).

questions.question: What is the 'Dangling Else' ambiguity in nested if statements resolved by in C?
questions.a: An 'else' always binds to the closest preceding unmatched 'if' in the same block scope
questions.b: An 'else' binds to the first 'if' in the file
questions.explanation: C grammar binds an else clause to the nearest inner unclosed if statement.

questions.question: What does the expression '(5 > 3) && (2 < 4)' evaluate to?
questions.explanation: Both sub-expressions (5 > 3) and (2 < 4) are true (1); 1 && 1 yields 1.

questions.question: What does the expression '(10 == 20) || (3 != 4)' evaluate to?
questions.explanation: (10 == 20) is false (0), but (3 != 4) is true (1); 0 || 1 yields 1.

questions.question: Why is using curly braces '{}' recommended even for single-line if-statement bodies?
questions.a: It prevents accidental macro expansion bugs and prevents logic errors when subsequent lines are added
questions.c: C compilers reject if statements without braces
questions.explanation: Braceless blocks are prone to maintenance errors (e.g. goto fail bug).

questions.question: What is the output of: int x = 0; if (x) printf("A"); else printf("B"); ?
questions.explanation: x is 0 (false), so the else branch executes and prints 'B'.

questions.question: How do you check if an integer 'num' is even in C?
questions.explanation: num % 2 yields 0 for even numbers and 1 (or -1) for odd numbers.

questions.question: What happens if a 'break;' statement is omitted at the end of a switch case block ('Fall-through')?
questions.b: Execution continues unconditionally into the statements of the next consecutive case
questions.c: The switch statement resets to case 1
questions.d: The compiler raises a fatal syntax error
questions.explanation: Without break, control falls through and executes following case blocks sequentially.

questions.question: What data types are legally permitted in a C switch expression?
questions.a: Only integer types (int, char, enum, short, long)
questions.explanation: Switch expressions in ISO C must evaluate to integral types or enumerations; floats and strings are prohibited.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'default:' label in a switch statement?
questions.a: It is executed first before any case
questions.b: It executes when none of the explicit 'case' constant values match the switch expression
questions.d: It is mandatory in every switch block
questions.explanation: default acts as a fallback catch-all when no case values match.

questions.question: Can case labels in a C switch statement contain variables (e.g. 'case x:')?
questions.a: Yes, any variable can be used
questions.b: No, case labels must be compile-time integer constant expressions (e.g. 'case 5:' or 'case 'A':')
questions.c: Yes, if the variable is declared global
questions.d: Only if using GCC compiler extensions
questions.explanation: Case labels must resolve to compile-time constant integer values.

questions.question: Can multiple case labels share a single code block in a switch statement?
questions.a: No, each case must have unique duplicate code
questions.b: Yes, by stacking case labels consecutively (e.g. case 'a': case 'A': doSomething(); break;)
questions.explanation: Stacking case labels allows multiple values to trigger the same action via intentional fallthrough.

questions.question: Can a switch statement contain duplicate case values (e.g. two 'case 1:' labels)?
questions.b: No, duplicate case values cause a compilation error
questions.c: Yes, only the first one executes
questions.explanation: Duplicate case constant expressions in the same switch block violate C grammar and fail to compile.

questions.question: What is 'Duff's Device' in advanced C programming?
questions.b: An unrolled loop optimization technique interleaving a switch statement inside a do-while loop
questions.c: A method to allocate virtual memory
questions.explanation: Duff's Device exploits switch case fall-through inside a loop for high-speed block data copying.

questions.question: Where can the 'default:' label be placed inside a switch block?
questions.a: Strictly at the very end only
questions.b: Anywhere inside the switch block (beginning, middle, or end)
questions.c: Strictly at the beginning before case labels
questions.d: It must be outside the switch braces
questions.explanation: default may appear anywhere inside the switch body, though placing it at the end is standard convention.

questions.question: Why is declaring a new variable with initialization directly inside a case label invalid without enclosing braces?
questions.a: Case labels are jump targets; jumping past variable initialization into scope violates C scoping rules
questions.b: Variables cannot be created inside switch statements
questions.c: Memory cannot be allocated in switch statements
questions.explanation: Jumping over a variable initialization causes scope errors; use '{ ... }' to create a distinct sub-block.

questions.question: What is the output of: int c = 2; switch(c) { case 1: printf("1"); case 2: printf("2"); case 3: printf("3"); } ?
questions.explanation: Matching case 2 prints '2', and without a break, falls through to case 3 to print '3', outputting '23'.

questions.question: What is the key functional difference between a 'while' loop and a 'do-while' loop?
questions.a: while tests condition before execution; do-while executes the loop body AT LEAST ONCE before evaluating the condition
questions.d: do-while does not support integer counters
questions.explanation: do-while is a post-test loop guaranteed to execute its body at least once.

questions.question: What does the 'continue;' statement do inside a loop body?
questions.b: Skips the remainder of the current iteration and jumps directly to the next loop iteration test/increment
questions.explanation: continue bypasses remaining statements in the current iteration and cycles to the next iteration step.

questions.question: What does the 'break;' statement do when encountered inside an active loop?
questions.a: Immediately terminates the innermost enclosing loop and transfers control to the statement following the loop
questions.explanation: break exits the innermost loop structure immediately.

questions.question: What constitutes an intentional infinite loop in C syntax?
questions.d: All of the above are valid infinite loops
questions.explanation: All three idioms create infinite loops in standard C.

questions.question: In a standard 'for (init; condition; increment)' loop, when is the increment expression executed?
questions.b: At the end of each iteration cycle, before re-testing the condition
questions.explanation: The increment step runs after the body statements complete in each iteration.

questions.question: In C99, is declaring loop counter variables inside the for header (e.g. 'for (int i = 0; ...)') permitted?
questions.a: No, variables must always be declared at the top of the function
questions.b: Yes, C99 introduced block-scoped loop declarations in for-loop headers
questions.explanation: C99 allows variable declarations directly inside the for loop initialization clause.

questions.question: What is an 'Off-by-One' error (OBOE) in loop index iteration?
questions.a: A logic error where a loop iterates one time too many or one time too few (e.g. using '<=' instead of '<')
questions.explanation: OBOE occurs when boundary limits are miscalculated by 1 index position.

questions.question: How many times will the loop 'for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)' execute its body?
questions.explanation: The loop runs for indices 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4 (exactly 5 iterations).

questions.question: What is loop unrolling in compiler optimization?
questions.a: Converting a loop into a recursive function
questions.b: Replicating the loop body multiple times to reduce loop control branching overhead and exploit instruction-level parallelism
questions.c: Removing all loops from source code
questions.explanation: Loop unrolling reduces jump/counter overhead by processing multiple array items per iteration.

questions.question: What happens if the condition in a 'while (condition)' loop is never modified inside the loop body and remains non-zero?
questions.a: The loop becomes an infinite loop and runs indefinitely
questions.b: The program automatically exits after 100 iterations
questions.explanation: Failure to update condition variables causes indefinite execution.

questions.question: In C, array indexing is based on which numbering system?
questions.explanation: Array elements in C are indexed from 0 to N-1.

questions.question: What is the memory layout of elements in a one-dimensional C array?
questions.b: Contiguous in memory (elements are stored sequentially one after another in a continuous block)
questions.d: Segmented across different CPU cache lines only
questions.explanation: Arrays are guaranteed to occupy contiguous memory locations.

questions.question: How is a 2D array 'int matrix[3][4]' laid out in physical memory in C?
questions.b: Row-major order (row 0 elements first, followed by row 1, then row 2)
questions.explanation: C stores multi-dimensional arrays in contiguous row-major order.

questions.question: What happens if you access an array out of bounds (e.g. accessing 'arr[10]' on an array of size 5) in C?
questions.b: It results in Undefined Behavior (may corrupt memory, read garbage data, or cause a Segmentation Fault)
questions.c: The array automatically resizes to 11 elements
questions.explanation: C does not perform automated array bounds checking at runtime.

questions.question: If an array is declared as 'int arr[5] = {1, 2};', what are the values of the remaining uninitialized elements?
questions.explanation: Partial initializer lists cause remaining elements to be zero-initialized.

questions.question: How do you calculate the number of elements in a statically declared array 'int arr[20]' in C?
questions.explanation: Dividing total array byte size by single element byte size yields element count.

questions.question: When an array name is passed as an argument to a function, what does it decay into?
questions.a: A complete duplicate copy of the entire array
questions.b: A pointer to its first element (pointer decay)
questions.explanation: Array identifiers decay into a pointer to element 0 when passed to functions.

questions.question: In C99, what is a Variable Length Array (VLA)?
questions.a: An array whose size is determined at runtime based on an integer variable value (allocated on the stack)
questions.b: An array that can grow dynamically like a vector
questions.c: An array stored in global memory
questions.explanation: VLAs allow stack allocation with runtime size expressions (e.g. int arr[n];).

questions.question: Can the size of a standard fixed-size stack array be modified after declaration in C?
questions.b: No, stack array sizes are fixed at compile time and cannot be resized
questions.explanation: Static array dimensions are immutable; dynamic resizing requires heap pointers with malloc/realloc.

questions.question: What is the value of '*(arr + 3)' identical to in array subscript notation?
questions.explanation: Array subscripting 'arr[i]' is syntactic sugar for '*(arr + i)'.

questions.question: What character is used to terminate strings in C?
questions.explanation: C strings are null-terminated character arrays ending with '\0'.

questions.question: Which standard library function calculates the length of a string (excluding the null terminator)?
questions.explanation: strlen() counts characters up to (but not including) the terminating '\0'.

questions.question: Why is the standard library function 'strcpy()' considered unsafe in modern C programming?
questions.a: It does not perform buffer bounds checking and can cause buffer overflow vulnerabilities if the source string exceeds the destination buffer
questions.d: It only works on ASCII characters
questions.explanation: strcpy() writes past buffer limits; strncpy() or safe alternatives should be used.

questions.question: Which function compares two strings lexicographically in C?
questions.explanation: strcmp() returns 0 if strings match, negative if str1 < str2, positive if str1 > str2.

questions.question: Which function concatenates (appends) a source string to the end of a destination string?
questions.explanation: strcat() appends source characters to the destination buffer.

questions.question: What does 'strcmp("apple", "banana")' return?
questions.explanation: Since 'apple' precedes 'banana' alphabetically, strcmp returns a negative value.

questions.question: What happens if you attempt to modify a string literal (e.g. 'char *s = "hello"; s[0] = 'H';') in C?
questions.b: It causes Undefined Behavior / Segmentation Fault because string literals are stored in read-only memory
questions.c: It creates a new string copy
questions.explanation: String literals reside in read-only data segments; mutating them triggers access violations.

questions.question: Which function safely writes formatted data into a character string buffer with size limits?
questions.explanation: snprintf() takes a max size parameter to strictly prevent buffer overruns.

questions.question: Which function finds the first occurrence of a character in a string?
questions.explanation: strchr() returns a pointer to the first occurrence of character c in string s, or NULL.

questions.question: Which function finds the first occurrence of a substring within another string in C?
questions.explanation: strstr() locates a target substring within a source string.

questions.question: Why must variable arguments passed to 'scanf()' be prefixed with the address-of operator '&' (e.g. 'scanf("%d", &x)')?
questions.a: Because scanf requires pointer memory addresses to write parsed input into the caller's variables
questions.explanation: C is pass-by-value; scanf must receive pointer addresses to mutate caller variables.

questions.question: Why was the standard 'gets()' function permanently removed in the ISO C11 standard?
questions.b: It lacked buffer size limits, making buffer overflow exploits unavoidable
questions.explanation: gets() is intrinsically insecure and was deprecated in C99 and removed in C11.

questions.question: Which safe function should be used instead of 'gets()' to read a line of text from standard input?
questions.explanation: fgets() specifies maximum buffer capacity and reads from stdin safely.

questions.question: What does 'getchar()' return when it reaches the end of the input stream?
questions.explanation: getchar() returns EOF (type int) upon reaching end of file or input error.

questions.question: What is the return value of 'scanf()' upon successful execution?
questions.a: The number of input items successfully matched and assigned
questions.b: The total number of characters read
questions.explanation: scanf() returns the count of successfully matched conversion items.

questions.question: What is the purpose of 'fflush(stdout)'?
questions.b: Flushes unwritten buffered output data immediately to the display console
questions.explanation: fflush(stdout) forces buffered stream output to be written immediately to the terminal.

questions.question: Which standard stream in C is dedicated for unbuffered diagnostic error messages?
questions.explanation: stderr (standard error) writes diagnostic logs unbuffered so errors appear even if program crashes.

questions.question: What happens when 'scanf("%s", str)' encounters whitespace (space, tab, or newline)?
questions.a: It includes the space in the string
questions.b: It stops reading and terminates the string with '\0'
questions.explanation: The %s specifier stops reading at the first whitespace character.

questions.question: Which function writes a single character to standard output?
questions.explanation: putchar() outputs a single character to stdout.

questions.question: How do you read a full line containing spaces using scanf safely?
questions.explanation:
The scanset %[^
] with a length limit reads all characters up to the newline character.

questions.question: What is a 'Function Prototype' (forward declaration) in C?
questions.a: The compiled binary of a function
questions.b: A declaration specifying the function's name, return type, and parameter types before its actual definition
questions.explanation: Prototypes inform the compiler of function signatures before call sites occur.

questions.question: In C, are function arguments passed by value or by reference by default?
questions.b: Pass by Value (a local copy of each argument is created in the function's stack frame)
questions.explanation: C exclusively uses pass-by-value; pass-by-reference is simulated by passing pointer addresses.

questions.question: What does the 'static' storage class specifier do when applied to a local variable inside a function?
questions.b: Preserves the variable's value across multiple function calls, maintaining static lifetime throughout program execution
questions.explanation: Static local variables retain their values across function invocations throughout program lifetime.

questions.question: What does the 'static' keyword do when applied to a global function or variable at file scope?
questions.a: Restricts its linkage and visibility strictly to that translation unit (file), preventing external access
questions.c: Exports it to all C files
questions.explanation: Internal linkage (static) hides functions and global variables from other source files.

questions.question: What is 'Recursion' in C programming?
questions.b: A programming technique where a function calls itself to solve smaller subproblems until reaching a base case
questions.explanation: Recursive functions call themselves until satisfying terminating base conditions.

questions.question: What fatal error occurs if a recursive function lacks a proper base case or recurses too deeply?
questions.a: Segmentation fault due to Stack Overflow (call stack exhaustion)
questions.explanation: Unbounded recursion exhausts stack memory allocation, triggering stack overflow crashes.

questions.question: What does the 'inline' function specifier suggest to the C compiler?
questions.b: Suggests replacing function calls with the actual body code to eliminate call overhead
questions.d: Force function to run in kernel mode
questions.explanation: inline advises the compiler to inline code at call sites to eliminate call frame overhead.

questions.question: What is the return type of a function that does not return any value?
questions.explanation: void denotes an absence of return value.

questions.question: Which standard header defines macros for handling variable-argument functions (variadic functions like printf)?
questions.explanation: <stdarg.h> provides va_list, va_start, va_arg, and va_end macros.

questions.question: What is a 'Pure Function' in software design?
questions.a: A function written without any comments
questions.b: A function whose return value depends solely on its input arguments, producing no observable side effects
questions.explanation: Pure functions produce deterministic output from inputs without mutating global state.

questions.question: What does the dereference operator '*' do when applied to a pointer variable (e.g. '*ptr')?
questions.b: Accesses or modifies the value stored at the memory address pointed to by the pointer
questions.c: Gets the address of the pointer itself
questions.explanation: *ptr accesses the target data value at the referenced memory address.

questions.question: What is a 'NULL' pointer in C?
questions.a: A pointer pointing to random heap data
questions.b: A pointer assigned a special reserved value (address 0) indicating it does not point to any valid memory object
questions.c: A pointer to a character array
questions.explanation: NULL indicates a non-pointing reference. Dereferencing NULL causes instant segmentation faults.

questions.question: What is a 'Dangling Pointer' in C memory management?
questions.a: A pointer pointing to a memory location that has already been deallocated (freed)
questions.b: A pointer with a value of NULL
questions.explanation: Dangling pointers reference invalidated memory, causing critical use-after-free bugs.

questions.question: What does Pointer Arithmetic 'ptr + 1' do on a pointer of type 'int *' (assuming 4-byte integers)?
questions.a: Adds 1 byte to the memory address
questions.b: Advances the memory address by sizeof(int) (4 bytes) to point to the next contiguous integer
questions.d: Increments the integer value stored at ptr
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic scales automatically by the byte size of the underlying target data type.

questions.question: What is a 'Void Pointer' (void *) in C?
questions.a: A pointer that cannot point to anything
questions.b: A generic, typeless pointer that can hold the memory address of any data type without type casting
questions.c: A pointer to a function returning void
questions.explanation: void * is a universal generic pointer type used in memory functions like malloc and memcpy.

questions.question: Which dynamic memory allocation function allocates a contiguous block of bytes from the heap WITHOUT initializing them?
questions.explanation: malloc(size) allocates uninitialized heap memory containing indeterminate garbage bytes.

questions.question: Which dynamic memory allocation function allocates memory and zeroes out all allocated bytes?
questions.explanation: calloc() allocates memory and initializes all bytes to zero.

questions.question: What is a 'Memory Leak' in C?
questions.b: When dynamically allocated heap memory (via malloc/calloc) is no longer referenced but never released with free(), consuming available RAM
questions.d: When a file is deleted from hard disk
questions.explanation: Memory leaks occur when allocated heap blocks are abandoned without calling free().

questions.question: What is the consequence of 'Double Free' (calling free() twice on the same memory pointer)?
questions.a: It frees the memory twice as fast
questions.b: It causes heap corruption and Undefined Behavior, often leading to security exploits or immediate crash
questions.explanation: Double free corrupts heap allocator metadata and is a major security vulnerability.

questions.question: What is a 'Function Pointer' in C?
questions.a: A pointer pointing to a variable in main()
questions.b: A pointer that stores the memory address of executable code (a function) allowing dynamic callback invocation
questions.c: A function that returns a pointer
questions.explanation: Function pointers store code addresses and enable callbacks and runtime polymorphism.

questions.question: Which operator is used to access struct members through a pointer to that struct (e.g. 'ptr->member')?
questions.explanation: Arrow operator 'ptr->x' is shorthand for '(*ptr).x'.

questions.question: What is 'Structure Padding' in C memory alignment?
questions.a: Adding comments inside a struct definition
questions.b: Unused bytes inserted by the compiler between struct members to align data types with natural hardware word boundaries for fast CPU access
questions.c: Compressing struct members to save disk space
questions.explanation: Compilers insert padding bytes so members align with CPU word boundaries (e.g. 4 or 8 bytes).

questions.question: What is the key difference between a 'struct' and a 'union' in C?
questions.a: In a struct, each member has its own separate memory; in a union, all members share the exact same memory location (size equals largest member)
questions.d: There is no difference in ISO C
questions.explanation: Unions overlay all member fields over the same shared memory offset.

questions.question: Which standard library function opens a file stream in C?
questions.explanation: fopen() opens a file and returns a FILE * stream handle, or NULL on failure.

questions.question: What does the file open mode '"rb"' specify in fopen()?
questions.a: Open file for writing in text mode
questions.b: Open an existing file for reading in binary mode
questions.explanation: "rb" opens an existing binary file for input reading without newline translation.

questions.question: Which function writes raw binary blocks of memory directly to a file stream?
questions.explanation: fwrite() writes raw binary buffers to streams.

questions.question: Which function reads raw binary data from a file stream into a memory buffer?
questions.explanation: fread() reads binary records from a file stream directly into memory.

questions.question: Which function repositions the file position indicator in a file stream to a specific byte offset?
questions.explanation: fseek() moves the stream file pointer relative to SEEK_SET, SEEK_CUR, or SEEK_END.

questions.question: What does 'ftell(stream)' return?
questions.a: The current byte position offset of the file indicator from the beginning of the file
questions.b: Total number of lines in the file
questions.explanation: ftell() reports the current file position offset in bytes.

questions.question: Why must 'fclose(stream)' always be called when file I/O operations are finished?
questions.a: To prevent file system corruption, flush cached output buffers, and release OS file descriptor handles
questions.b: To delete the file from disk
questions.d: It is optional and does nothing
questions.explanation: Closing files flushes remaining buffer caches and releases OS handle resources.

questions.question: Which standard library function dynamically changes the size of previously allocated heap memory?
questions.explanation: realloc() expands or contracts existing heap allocations, migrating data if necessary.

questions.question: What is the safe idiom for realloc() to prevent memory leaks if realloc() fails and returns NULL?
questions.a: Assign directly to original pointer: 'ptr = realloc(ptr, new_size);'
questions.b: Use a temporary pointer: 'void *tmp = realloc(ptr, new_size); if (tmp) ptr = tmp;'
questions.explanation: If realloc fails, assigning directly to ptr overwrites the pointer with NULL, leaking the original block.

questions.question: Which standard header must be included to use mathematical functions like sqrt(), pow(), and sin()?
questions.explanation: <math.h> declares standard floating-point trigonometric and algebraic functions.

questions.question: When compiling a C program using <math.h> with GCC on Linux/Unix, which linker flag must be passed?
questions.explanation: -lm instructs the linker to link the system math library (libm.so/libm.a).

questions.question: Which function computes the square root of a double value in C?
questions.explanation: sqrt(x) computes the non-negative square root of x.

questions.question: What does 'pow(2.0, 3.0)' evaluate to in <math.h>?
questions.explanation: pow(x, y) raises x to the power y (2^3 = 8.0).

questions.question: Which function in <math.h> rounds a floating-point number UP to the nearest integer?
questions.explanation: ceil(3.2) returns 4.0 (smallest integer greater than or equal to x).

questions.question: Which function in <math.h> rounds a floating-point number DOWN to the nearest integer?
questions.explanation: floor(3.8) returns 3.0 (largest integer less than or equal to x).

questions.question: Which function computes the absolute value of an integer in <stdlib.h>?
questions.explanation: abs() is for integers (<stdlib.h>); fabs() is for floating-point doubles (<math.h>).

questions.question: What does 'qsort()' from <stdlib.h> require as its 4th argument?
questions.b: A pointer to a comparator function: 'int (*compar)(const void *, const void *)'
questions.explanation: qsort() is a generic quicksort routine taking a comparator callback.

questions.question: What are 'Header Guards' (#ifndef HEADER_H, #define HEADER_H, #endif) used for in C?
questions.b: To prevent multiple redundant inclusions of the same header file during preprocessing
questions.d: To speed up runtime CPU execution
questions.explanation: Header guards prevent redefinition errors when headers are included transitively.

questions.question: What is '#pragma once' in modern C compilers?
questions.a: A non-standard but universally supported preprocessor directive serving as a concise header guard
questions.b: A command to compile the file only once in lifetime
questions.explanation: #pragma once ensures the compiler includes the header file only once per translation unit.

questions.question: What is a 'Segmentation Fault' (SIGSEGV) in C programs?
questions.b: An operating system signal raised when a program attempts to access a memory address it does not have permission to read or write
questions.explanation: SIGSEGV is triggered by invalid memory accesses like dereferencing NULL or out-of-bounds writes.

questions.question: What is a 'Buffer Overflow' and why is it a critical security risk?
questions.a: When a program writes data beyond the allocated boundary of a buffer, corrupting adjacent stack memory or return addresses
questions.b: When the hard drive fills up completely
questions.c: When video graphics buffer runs out of VRAM
questions.d: When too many print statements execute
questions.explanation: Buffer overflows can overwrite stack frames and enable arbitrary code execution exploits.

questions.question: What tool is widely used on Linux to detect memory leaks, uninitialized memory reads, and out-of-bounds heap accesses in C programs?
questions.explanation: Valgrind Memcheck dynamically detects heap memory leaks, invalid frees, and memory corruptions.

questions.question: What does the GCC flag '-Wall -Wextra -Werror' do during compilation?
questions.b: Enables all comprehensive warnings and treats all warnings as fatal errors, enforcing clean code standards
questions.c: Generates release binaries without debugging symbols
questions.explanation: Enabling strict warning flags catches subtle bugs, uninitialized variables, and type mismatches.

questions.question: What is a 'Makefile' in software engineering?
questions.a: A text file containing build targets, dependencies, and shell compiler rules executed by the 'make' automation utility
questions.b: A file containing raw machine code
questions.explanation: Makefiles automate modular compilation based on file modification timestamps.

questions.question: What is the difference between static linking and dynamic linking in C?
questions.a: Static linking bundles library code directly into the executable binary; dynamic linking links shared libraries (.so/.dll) at runtime
questions.b: Static linking only works on Windows
questions.c: Dynamic linking is slower to write
questions.explanation: Static binaries are self-contained; dynamic binaries share library memory across running processes.

questions.question: What is the 'Stack' vs 'Heap' memory in C program architecture?
questions.a: Stack is automatically managed fast memory for local function variables; Heap is manually managed dynamic memory for lifetime-controlled allocations
questions.b: Stack is stored on disk; Heap is stored in CPU cache
questions.c: Stack is unlimited; Heap is 1 MB
questions.d: There is no difference in architecture
questions.explanation: Stack frames are managed by function calls/returns; heap memory is allocated/freed manually via malloc/free.

questions.question: What does the 'volatile' type qualifier tell the C compiler?
questions.a: The variable can never be changed
questions.b: The variable may be modified unexpectedly by external hardware or concurrent threads, preventing compiler optimization caching
questions.c: The variable is stored on the GPU
questions.explanation: volatile forces direct memory reads/writes every time, bypassing register caching in memory-mapped I/O.

questions.question: What is 'Undefined Behavior' (UB) in the ISO C standard?
questions.b: Code execution for which the C standard imposes no requirements; the program may crash, produce garbage output, or appear to work unpredictably
questions.c: A feature reserved for future C versions
questions.explanation: UB allows compilers to assume illegal conditions never occur, leading to aggressive optimizations and unpredictable bugs.

questions.question: What is the 'Strict Aliasing Rule' in C?
questions.a: Pointers of different incompatible types cannot point to the same memory location, allowing compilers to assume their dereferences do not interfere
questions.d: Pointers cannot be cast to void *
questions.explanation: Strict aliasing permits register caching by assuming different type pointers do not alias the same memory.

questions.question: What does AddressSanitizer (ASan) flag '-fsanitize=address' do when compiling with modern GCC/Clang?
questions.b: Instruments compiled code with fast memory error detection for out-of-bounds access, use-after-free, and stack bugs
questions.explanation: ASan detects memory safety violations at runtime with minimal performance overhead.

questions.question: What is a 'Race Condition' in multi-threaded C programming using POSIX threads (pthread)?
questions.a: A competition between two CPU cores
questions.b: When two or more concurrent threads access shared memory simultaneously and at least one access is a write without synchronization (mutex)
questions.c: When a loop runs faster than expected
questions.explanation: Data races corrupt shared state; mutex locks or atomic operations are required to serialize access.

questions.question: What does the 'restrict' keyword (introduced in C99) signify when qualifying a pointer parameter?
questions.b: The pointer is the sole exclusive reference to the object it points to within that scope, enabling aggressive compiler vectorization
questions.c: The pointer cannot be passed to other functions
questions.d: The pointer is allocated on stack
questions.explanation: restrict informs the optimizer that no other pointer will access the same memory block.

questions.question: What is an 'Atomic Operation' in concurrent C programming (stdatomic.h)?
questions.a: An operation that uses nuclear computing
questions.b: An indivisible memory read-modify-write operation that executes completely without possibility of interruption or data race from other threads
questions.explanation: Atomic instructions execute as a single indivisible hardware step without mutex locking.

questions.question: Why is modifying a global variable inside an asynchronous Signal Handler considered hazardous in C?
questions.a: Signals can interrupt execution at any instruction; non-atomic signal modifications cause data corruption unless typed as 'volatile sig_atomic_t'
questions.explanation: Only async-signal-safe functions and volatile sig_atomic_t variables can be safely modified in signal handlers.

questions.question: What is 'Memory Alignment' and why does unaligned memory access cause performance penalties or hardware faults on ARM/MIPS CPUs?
questions.a: CPUs fetch data in multi-byte word chunks; accessing data across word boundaries requires multiple memory bus cycles or triggers hardware alignment faults
questions.d: Unaligned access causes hard drive fragmentation
questions.explanation: CPUs access memory efficiently when addresses are multiples of natural data sizes (2, 4, 8 bytes).

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'setjmp()' and 'longjmp()' functions in <setjmp.h>?
questions.a: To allocate jump tables in heap
questions.b: To perform non-local jumps (unwinding stack frames across functions) for low-level exception handling and error recovery
questions.explanation: setjmp saves execution context and longjmp restores it, jumping across stack frames.

questions.question: What is a 'Zero-Day Vulnerability' frequently rooted in C memory unsafety?
questions.a: A bug that takes 0 days to fix
questions.b: A previously unknown software security flaw (such as a remote heap buffer overflow or use-after-free) exploited before developers release a patch
questions.explanation: C memory safety vulnerabilities are prime targets for zero-day remote code execution exploits.
